newsitem.title: POLAND: Foreigners storm Polish bond tender, push zloty up.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners storm Polish bond tender, push zloty up.

text.p: Foreign investors stormed into Polish treasuries at Thursday's 700 million zloty 16-percent two-year and 12-percent five-year fixed bond primary auction and pushed the zloty to record highs, dealers said.

They said interest in Polish paper, especially longer-term bonds, picked up after better-than-expected 1996 inflation stopped speculation about a near-term official rate rise and after Poland presented a plan of how it wanted to join the EMU.

"Foreign investors were very active at today's auction, bidding especially for the 5-year bond, suggesting that their long-term view on Poland is good," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, debt dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.
Some dealers said foreigners may have bought as much as 60 percent of the 518 million zlotys sold at today's bond auction.
At the tender the treasury cut the minimum price of the five year bond to 79.90 from 80.50 on December 19, 1997. It lowered the 2-year paper's minimum price to 92.90 from 93.16.
Earlier this week Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said Poland stood a chance of meeting all EMU criteria and benefitting from full European integration early next century.

Kolodko said integration as early as 2004 would mean that Poland would give up its exchange rate policy, which presently devalues the zloty one percent per month against a basket, as a macro-economic tool and yield monetary policy making powers.
"Foreign investors are searching for longer paper...and Poland is a relatively stable country with EMU ambitions," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior treasury dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Capital inflows from foreign investor entry into Polish paper also pushed the zloty to an all-time high, since its December 1995 one-off appreciation, against the basket of five western currencies on Thursday.
Dealers said the zloty's run, which propelled it to new highs at 3.63/3.53 percent from the trading band centre against Wednesday's close at 3.43/3.34 percent, may continue on Friday.

"The market's currency selling trend is likely to continue, taking the zloty closer to four percent from parity, if the central bank does not halt the climb with an intervention," said one senior dealer at a foreign bank in Warsaw.
The zloty closed at 2.9000/30 against the dollar, up from 2.9095/05 on Wednesday and at 1.8205/25 to the mark, flat from 1.8215/25.
